extracted.intended_audience: health journalists, news editors, media researchers, and journalism trainers
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric and evaluation procedure for assessing US news stories that make claims about the efficacy or safety of treatments, tests, products, or procedures; used to grade completeness, balance, and quality of reporting. Applies to reviews of newspaper, magazine, wire, and TV health stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately discusses costs.
rubrics_metrics.description: We believe that, in an era when health care spending represents 16% of the US gross domestic product, a story is incomplete if it does not address the costs of an approach, and a comparison with existing alternatives. We also think journalists should explore whether insurers are likely to pay for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should address costs of the intervention and compare costs with existing alternatives; discuss insurability and likelihood insurers will pay. Failure to mention costs renders a story incomplete given the economic impact of health care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifies benefits.
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should give some sense of the size of the potential benefits of the approach being discussed. Stories (and studies, for that matter) should also explain the benefits in absolute, not just relative, terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require numeric quantification of benefits and explicit presentation of absolute measures (not only relative percentages). Explain magnitude so consumers understand practical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately explains and quantifies potential harms.
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should give a complete picture of potential harms of an approach, and quantify those potential harms in absolute terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should describe types of harms and provide absolute risk figures. Omitting harms or failing to quantify them leads to unbalanced reporting and may mislead consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compares the new idea with existing alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.description: We expect that a story would put the new approach being discussed into the context of existing alternatives, with some discussion of the possible advantages or disadvantages of the new approach compared with existing alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize the new product/procedure by describing alternatives and how the new approach differs in benefits, harms, cost, availability, and evidence quality. Avoid presenting the new idea as the only option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeks out independent sources and discloses potential conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.description: We expect, just as the Association of Health Care Journalists does, that journalists should 'recognize that most stories involve a degree of nuance and complexity that no single source could provide. To reflect only one perspective of only one source is not wise; [journalists should] be vigilant in selecting sources, asking about, weighing and disclosing relevant financial, advocacy, personal or other interests of those [they] interview as a routine part of story research and interviews'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple independent sources rather than single-source stories. Routinely ask about and disclose financial ties, advocacy roles, personal interests, and other conflicts. Verify industry-provided claims with independent experts or studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoids disease mongering.
rubrics_metrics.description: This criterion is an attempt to help journalists avoid promulgating the medicalization of normal states of or variations in health (e.g., baldness, menstruation, short stature, etc.). We also try to educate journalists about surrogate endpoints and about how risk factors are not diseases. With this criterion, we also remind them not to exaggerate the prevalence or incidence of a condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about labeling normal life variations as diseases; avoid exaggerating prevalence/incidence. Explain difference between risk factors, surrogate endpoints, and actual disease outcomes. Watch for promotion that creates unnecessary demand for interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews the study methodology or the quality of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.description: The story should reflect an understanding that not all studies are equal. If a story does not point out some of the limitations of an observational study and does not caution about interpreting uncontrolled data, for example, we will judge it unsatisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and report study design, limitations (e.g., observational vs randomized, sample size, follow-up, manufacturer funding), and generalizability. Explain how study quality affects confidence in findings rather than treating all studies as equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishes the true novelty of the idea.
rubrics_metrics.description: Many 'new' products or procedures are not really novel. The product reported may be the sixth new member of a well-established class of drugs. It may be a device that has only been judged to be substantially equivalent to other devices already on the market. Journalists should accurately reflect the novelty (or lack thereof) of 'new' products or procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify whether a development is genuinely novel or incremental. Place it in the context of prior products, classes, or approvals; check regulatory determination (e.g., substantial equivalence) and existing evidence from earlier iterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishes the availability of the product or procedure.
rubrics_metrics.description: Many stories report on products or procedures that are still in clinical trials. We expect journalists to explain whether something is only available via limited access in clinical trials, whether something is FDA approved, whether insurability limits availability, etc. Many news stories seem to treat FDA approval of an investigational drug as a fait accompli, making predictions about how the drug 'could be' or 'should be' approved and on the market within a given time frame. Such stories would be rated as unsatisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report whether the intervention is experimental, available only in trials, FDA approved, commercially available, or subject to insurance/coverage limitations. Avoid speculative timelines about approval and market availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appears not to rely solely or largely on a news release.
rubrics_metrics.description: We expect, just as the Association of Health Care Journalists does, that journalists should 'Preserve journalistic independence by avoiding the use of video news releases or the use of quotes from printed news releases; label and credit the source whenever a portion of a video or printed news release is used'. We expect a journalist to use a news release for background information only, and to then seek independent experts to comment on a development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base a story primarily on a news release. Use releases only as background; seek independent verification and commentary. Clearly label and credit any release content that is used. Stories relying mainly on releases are rated unsatisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for review (story scope).
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to be eligible for review, a story must include a claim of efficacy or safety in a health care product or procedure (drug, device, diagnostic or screening test, surgical procedure, dietary recommendation, vitamin, supplement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only stories that assert efficacy or safety claims for treatments/tests/products/procedures are evaluated using this rubric. Routine health stories without such claims may be not applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating categories and reviewer process.
rubrics_metrics.description: For each criterion, the story is given a rating of 'satisfactory,' 'unsatisfactory,' or 'not applicable.' Three reviewers—with backgrounds in medicine, health services research, public health, or journalism—analyze each article. The publisher author acts as the third reviewer and mediates disagreements to reach consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use three independent reviewers with relevant expertise; classify each criterion as satisfactory/unsatisfactory/not applicable; resolve disagreements by mediation and consensus. Inter-reviewer reliability observed (average percent agreement across ten criteria was 74% in a random sample). Publish reviewer identities and be transparent about methods.
